newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: New Pakistan government seen cooperating with IMF.
newsitem.headline: New Pakistan government seen cooperating with IMF.

text.p: Pakistan's new government will cooperate with the International Monetary Fund but may try to persuade it to relax some of its economic targets, analysts said on Wednesday.
A visiting IMF team is due to complete a review of Pakistan's economic performance by March 21 to decide whether to disburse the next $122 million tranche of a standby loan.

"In our view, despite some statements made by the prime minister, he and his finance minister will not part ways with the IMF," Muddassar Malik, senior analyst at BMA Capital Management, told Reuters.

He said statements by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz casting doubts on Pakistan's ability to meet some IMF-agreed targets "should be seen as no more than a negotiating posture adopted by a popularly elected government".

Sharif, who swept to power after a landslide election win on February 3, has pledged to revive industry and stimulate export-led growth to rescue the ailing economy, but some analysts say his priorities may conflict with those of the IMF.

"We consider it very likely that the new government will abandon the budget deficit target of four percent (of gross domestic product) set by its predecessor and go for a more achievable target of five to 5.5 percent," Anisur Rehman, research head at SocGen-Crosby Securities, said.
A caretaker government promised in December to cut the budget gap to four percent of GDP from 6.3 percent in 1995/96 to meet IMF conditions for resumption of a stalled standby loan.
Rehman said Sharif was expected to agree to accelerate the import tariff reduction programme to a maximum of 50 percent from 60 percent in the June budget for 1997/98 (July-June).

Sharif, seen as pro-business, might improve tax collection by convincing more businessmen to pay tax, he said. He might find it easier than his predecessor Benazir Bhutto, a big landlord, to broaden the tax base and increase farm tax.

Rehman said reducing the fiscal deficit even to 5.5 percent of GDP could result in slashing government borrowing from banks for budgetary support to 42 billion rupees ($1.044 billion) from the current estimated level of more than 70 billion rupees.

"We also expect the military expenditure to be curtailed in real terms at least," he said. "The improvement in fiscal balance and the reduction in tariffs will result in the reinstatement of the IMF lending programme," he said.

Pakistan wants to negotiate an enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF) with the IMF to gain access to cheaper funds than are available under the standby arrangement, which expires in September.
"Considering the commitment of the newly elected government to solving the country's economic and debt problem, the IMF is expected to be cooperative in negotiations with the government," Malik said.
Sharif, with a clear political mandate and the support of the business community, was better placed than his predecessors to address Pakistan's long-term economic imbalances, he said.
